final_message:
Make the Most of Your School Days

I want to say a word to you about the use of your time while you are here. There is no one among you who does not wish to get something worth having out of these school days. But wishing is not enough. The days go by very fast, and unless we take hold of them one at a time, we shall find, when the year has ended, that a great many of them have slipped away from us without leaving anything behind.

In the first place, learn to be regular and prompt. Be in your place at the hour appointed, whether it is in the class-room, at the table, or at work. The student who forms the habit of being a few minutes late for everything will find, sooner or later, that he has formed the habit of being late for the opportunities of life. The world does not wait for such persons. It goes on, and leaves them behind.

In the second place, do not despise the small duties. Some of you, I fear, think that the real work of life lies somewhere in the future, and that the sweeping of a room, the care of a tool, or the learning of a single lesson is hardly worth your best effort. I want you to put that notion out of your minds. It is just in proportion as you do the little things well that you will be trusted with the large ones. I have never known a man to do a great thing well who had not first learned to do a small thing well.

In the third place, make the most of your teachers and of one another. Your teachers have given their lives to this work, and they are anxious to help you. Go to them with your difficulties. Do not be ashamed to ask a question, and do not be ashamed to confess that you do not understand. The only thing of which you should be ashamed is to go on year after year pretending to know what you do not know. And among your fellow-students, choose those friends whose influence will lift you up, and not those who will pull you down.

Finally, remember that you are here for a purpose. Your parents, and perhaps many friends, have made sacrifices that you might have this opportunity. Let us see to it that not a single week is wasted, and that when the term is over, we can look back upon it, each one of us, with a clear conscience, and say that we did the best we could. There is nothing, then, to be discouraged about. If you will do this, the future will take care of itself.
